title: THE GOSPEL DOES NOT DIVIDE HUMANITY INTO “CLEAN PEOPLE” AND “DIRTY PEOPLE”
paragraphs: THE GOSPEL DOES NOT DIVIDE HUMANITY INTO “CLEAN PEOPLE” AND “DIRTY PEOPLE”
Jesus did not come to congratulate the respectable and dispose of the ruined. He came because every one of us needs a Savior—and at the cross, the ground beneath our feet is terrifyingly level.
There is a kind of Christianity that knows how to stay clean without knowing how to love.
It knows which people to avoid.
Which scandals to whisper about.
Which sins are acceptable enough to mention in testimony and which ones make everybody uncomfortable.
It knows how to look at the addict and quietly think, At least I’m not like that.
It knows how to hear about the adulterer and say, How could someone do that?

It knows how to see the prisoner, the prostitute, the drunk, the sexually broken, the angry, the doubter, the backslider, the tattooed stranger, the pregnant unmarried woman, the divorced father, the ashamed teenager, the person walking into church after destroying almost everything in their life...
...and unconsciously divide the room.
Clean people over here.
Dirty people over there.
But there is a devastating problem.
That is not the Gospel.
And Jesus once told a story aimed directly at people who thought it was.
Luke tells us that Jesus addressed certain people who “trusted in themselves that they were righteous, and despised others” (Luke 18:9).
That sentence should make religious people uncomfortable.
Because Jesus did not describe atheists.
He described people confident in their own righteousness.
Then Jesus placed two men in the temple.
One was a Pharisee.
One was a tax collector.

To modern ears, “Pharisee” almost automatically sounds like the villain. That can make us miss the force of the story. In Jesus’ setting, the Pharisee represented visible religious seriousness, while tax collectors could be associated with exploitation and collaboration with Roman power.
In other words, if you had been standing nearby, you might have assumed you already knew which man God approved.
The Pharisee prayed:
“God, I thank thee, that I am not as other men are...” (Luke 18:11, KJV).
Listen carefully.
He thanked God...
and then used another human being as the background against which he could admire himself.
That is one of the most frightening forms of pride because it can sound like worship.
You can mention God while worshiping your own goodness.
You can thank God while despising the person beside you.
You can know Scripture and still use someone else’s failure to make yourself feel holy.
You can condemn sins Jesus condemns while secretly committing another sin Jesus condemns—self-righteousness.
Then Jesus turns our attention toward the other man.
The tax collector does not perform.
He does not negotiate.
He does not produce a résumé.
Jesus says he stood “afar off.”
He would not even lift his eyes toward heaven.
He beat his chest.
And then came one of the most desperate prayers in Scripture:
“God be merciful to me a sinner.” (Luke 18:13, KJV)
The Greek is striking:
Ὁ Θεός, ἱλάσθητί μοι τῷ ἁμαρτωλῷ.
Ho Theos, hilasthēti moi tō hamartōlō.
The man has stopped comparing himself with everybody else.
He has nowhere to hide.
No one else to blame.
No religious costume strong enough to cover what he knows about himself.
Just...
God.
Mercy.
Me.
The sinner.
And Jesus says something that would have shattered the expectations of His listeners:
“I tell you, this man went down to his house justified rather than the other...” (Luke 18:14, KJV).
The broken man asking for mercy went home justified.
The religious man admiring himself did not.
That is scandalous grace.
And before we turn the Pharisee into another “dirty person” so that we can congratulate ourselves for not being like him, we need to notice the trap.
The moment you say, Thank God I’m not self-righteous like that Pharisee, you may have climbed into his seat.
That is how deep our problem goes.
The Gospel does not divide humanity into good people who deserve Jesus and bad people who need Jesus.
Scripture draws the line somewhere much more devastating.
“All have sinned, and come short of the glory of God.” (Romans 3:23, KJV)
The Greek word translated “all” is πάντες — pantes.
All.
Not merely the visibly ruined.
Not merely people with criminal records.
Not merely people whose sins became public.
All.
The gossip and the adulterer.
The proud and the promiscuous.
The greedy and the addicted.
The church member and the church avoider.
The preacher and the prisoner.
The person ashamed of what happened last night and the person secretly proud of forty years of respectable living.
All have sinned.
But this does not mean Scripture pretends that sin is harmless or that every action has identical earthly consequences.
Jesus never needed to redefine evil in order to love sinners.
Biblical grace is not God looking at sin and saying, “It doesn't matter.”
Grace is infinitely more costly than that.
Sin mattered enough for Christ to go to the cross.
This is where Christianity becomes unlike mere moral self-improvement.
The Gospel does not say, “Clean yourself until God can tolerate you.”
It says Christ came for sinners.
Paul writes:
While we were still sinners.
Not after the rehabilitation.
Not after everybody respected us again.
Not after we finally conquered every temptation.
Not after we repaired our reputation.
Christ died for sinners.
There is an ancient Hebrew word that helps us understand the heart of this mercy.
חֶסֶד — ḥesed.
The word carries a rich range of meaning in the Old Testament involving steadfast love, covenant faithfulness, mercy, and loyal love. No single English word captures every use perfectly.
David knew something about needing that mercy.
After adultery, deception, abuse of power, and the arranged death of Uriah, David did not come before God pretending that reputation management could rescue him.
Psalm 51 opens:
“Have mercy upon me, O God, according to thy lovingkindness...” (Psalm 51:1, KJV)
The Hebrew includes:
חָנֵּנִי אֱלֹהִים כְּחַסְדֶּךָ
ḥonnēni Elohim keḥasdeka...
David's hope was not, “God, look how good I actually am.”
His hope was God's mercy.
And David did not call evil good.
He confessed.
“For I acknowledge my transgressions: and my sin is ever before me.” (Psalm 51:3, KJV)
This is where modern people sometimes misunderstand grace.
Grace does not eliminate repentance.
Grace makes repentance possible without despair.
Because repentance is not paying Jesus back.
It is turning from sin toward the One who alone can save you.
The New Testament word μετάνοια — metanoia refers to repentance, a turning or change of mind with moral and spiritual significance.
Jesus did not walk through the world telling broken people, “Remain exactly as you are because transformation would be judgmental.”
Neither did He say, “Transform yourself first, then perhaps I will receive you.”
He called sinners to Himself.
He forgave.
He restored.
He commanded repentance.
He transformed lives.
That balance matters.
Look at the woman dragged before Jesus in John 8.
Her accusers reduced her to her worst known act.
She became a case.
A scandal.
A weapon.
A public spectacle.
They said she had been caught in adultery.
They wanted judgment.
Jesus exposed something they desperately wanted hidden: the moral superiority of the accusers was not as secure as they imagined.
“He that is without sin among you, let him first cast a stone at her.” (John 8:7, KJV)
One after another, they left.
Then Jesus spoke to the woman.
“Neither do I condemn thee: go, and sin no more.” (John 8:11, KJV)
Do not separate those words.
“Neither do I condemn thee.”
Grace.
“Go, and sin no more.”
Transformation.
Jesus neither joined the mob nor celebrated the sin.
That is the Gospel-shaped tension our generation desperately needs.
Truth without grace can become a stone in a religious hand.
Grace without truth can become permission to remain enslaved.
But in Jesus Christ, grace and truth meet.
Maybe this is becoming uncomfortable because you know what it feels like to be the person everyone remembers for the worst chapter.
Maybe your marriage failed.
Maybe pornography has been eating away at your soul while everybody thinks you are fine.
Maybe you cheated.
Maybe you lied.
Maybe you betrayed somebody who trusted you.
Maybe alcohol has become the thing you reach for when nobody is watching.
Maybe you abandoned your faith and now feel too ashamed to return.
Maybe you had an abortion and have carried grief or guilt you have never told anyone about.
Maybe you have been sexually broken in ways you cannot explain without crying.
Maybe you have screamed at God.
Maybe you have sat in church singing about freedom while privately wondering whether Jesus could possibly want somebody who has done what you have done.
Or perhaps your darkness looks more respectable.
Maybe your addiction is approval.
Maybe your drug is being admired.
Maybe you secretly enjoy hearing that someone failed because their collapse makes your life look better.
Maybe you forgive only when people suffer enough first.
Maybe you have learned Christian vocabulary without developing Christlike mercy.
Maybe nobody would call your sin scandalous.
Maybe that is precisely why you have never confessed it.
Listen.
The cross destroys both kinds of boasting.
The openly broken person cannot say, “My sin does not matter.”
The outwardly respectable person cannot say, “I do not need mercy.”
At Calvary, both mouths are silenced.
And then...
both are invited.
This is why Paul could write:
The Greek begins:
Οὐδὲν ἄρα νῦν κατάκριμα...
Ouden ara nyn katakrima...
“Therefore now no condemnation...”
Do not confuse that with “no conviction.”
The Holy Spirit convicts.
God disciplines His children.
Scripture confronts sin.
But condemnation and conviction do not perform the same work.
Condemnation says, “There is no hope for someone like you.”
The Gospel says, “Run to Christ.”
Condemnation says, “Hide.”
Grace brings you into the light.
Condemnation chains your identity permanently to what you did.
The Gospel joins the repentant believer to Christ.
That does not erase consequences.
It does not magically repair every relationship.
It does not require victims to pretend they were never wounded.
Forgiveness is not permission for abuse to continue, and Christian mercy does not mean abandoning wisdom, justice, accountability, or appropriate boundaries.
But the Gospel declares something astonishing:
Your sin does not have greater saving power than the blood of Jesus.
Paul knew this personally.
Before he became the apostle who proclaimed Christ across the Roman world, he persecuted Christians.
He later described himself as a blasphemer, persecutor, and violent man.
Then he wrote:
“Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners; of whom I am chief.” (1 Timothy 1:15, KJV)
Paul's past was not rewritten by pretending it never happened.
Jesus rewrote what his past would ultimately mean.
Persecutor became preacher.
Enemy became servant.
Shame became testimony.
That is what Jesus does.
He does not merely improve reputations.
He raises the spiritually dead.
And perhaps the most dangerous person reading this is not the person crying because they know they have sinned.
It may be the person who still believes this article is mainly about somebody else.
Someone came into your mind when you read the title, didn't they?
The relative who embarrassed the family.
The Christian who fell publicly.
The person whose sexual sin disgusts you.
The addict who relapsed again.
The hypocrite.
The criminal.
The person whose theology irritates you.
The person whose life makes you uncomfortable.
Now comes the question we would rather avoid:
When you look at them, do you see a category...
or a soul?
Because Jesus ate with people respectable religion despised.
In Mark 2, scribes questioned why He ate with tax collectors and sinners.
Jesus answered:
“They that are whole have no need of the physician, but they that are sick...” (Mark 2:17, KJV)
Then:
“I came not to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance.” (Mark 2:17, KJV)
A hospital that despises sick people has forgotten why it exists.
And a church that has room only for people who already look healed has forgotten the Gospel.
This does not mean the church should tolerate unrepentant abuse, exploitation, deception, predatory behavior, or destructive sin.
It means accountability should aim toward truth, repentance, protection, restoration where possible, and holiness—not self-righteous entertainment at another person's collapse.
Galatians 6:1 tells spiritually mature believers to restore someone caught in transgression “in the spirit of meekness,” while watching themselves lest they also be tempted.
Restore.
Gently.
Watch yourself.
The Gospel leaves very little room for swagger.
Imagine what would happen if our churches actually believed this.
The alcoholic could say, “I need help,” before losing everything.
The pornography-addicted husband could confess before the secret devoured his marriage.
The exhausted pastor could admit he is struggling before becoming another headline.
The teenager wrestling with shame could approach a mature believer without wondering whether confession would become gossip.
The woman carrying decades of regret could finally discover that the blood of Jesus is stronger than the voice accusing her at three in the morning.
And religious people could stop pretending that polished appearances are the same thing as holiness.
Maybe that person is you.
Maybe you have spent years believing there are two kinds of people:
people God could love...
and people like you.
Hear the Gospel.
Jesus knew what He was purchasing at the cross.
He was not deceived about you.
He did not discover your history after Calvary.
He does not need you to edit your testimony before approaching Him.
Come into the light.
Confess.
Repent.
Believe.
Receive mercy.
Follow Christ.
Let Him begin rebuilding what sin shattered.
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.” (1 John 1:9, KJV)
Notice who does the cleansing.
He does.
Christianity is not dirty people scrubbing themselves hard enough to become worthy of Jesus.
It is sinners being washed, justified, sanctified, and transformed through the saving work of Christ.
Paul reminded the Corinthian believers of lives marked by serious sin and then said:
“And such were some of you: but ye are washed, but ye are sanctified, but ye are justified...” (1 Corinthians 6:11, KJV)
Ἀλλὰ ἀπελούσασθε...
Alla apelousasthe...
“But you were washed...”
Those words contain an entire resurrection.
Were.
Not because sin became acceptable.
Because Jesus changes people.
This is why the theme of Gospel Warrior is not “From Scandal to Respectability.”
It is not “From Bad Reputation to Good Reputation.”
It is not “From Dirty People to People Who Can Now Look Down on Dirty People.”
It is:
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
The Gospel does not give the redeemed permission to become the new Pharisees.
If Jesus pulled you from the pit, your testimony should make you more compassionate toward people still screaming from the bottom.
If Christ forgave you, forgiveness should astonish you.
If Christ washed you, you should never forget Who supplied the water.
If Christ carried your cross, you have no grounds for boasting except in Him.
So perhaps today you need to stop running.
Or perhaps you need to put down your stone.
Maybe you are the tax collector whispering, “God, have mercy on me.”
Maybe you are the Pharisee who suddenly realizes pride has been wearing religious clothing.
Maybe you are the woman surrounded by accusers.
Maybe you are one of the accusers.
There is room at the feet of Jesus for repentance.
That is the miracle.
Not affirmation of everything we have done.
Not denial of holiness.
Not cheap grace.
A crucified Savior.
An empty tomb.
Mercy purchased at immeasurable cost.
Forgiveness offered to sinners.
A new life that begins not when we finally become impressive enough for God...
but when we stop pretending we can save ourselves.
If something in this exposed what you have been hiding, do not turn this into another article you read, felt, and forgot.
Talk to Jesus.
And be honest.
Somebody reading silently may desperately need evidence that failure does not have to be the final chapter when a sinner turns to Jesus.
Not because an article can save you.
It cannot.
Give them the chance to hear about Jesus.
Christ alone saves.

Following Gospel Warrior can help you stay connected to daily Scripture, biblical truth, conviction, encouragement, healing, discipleship, and spiritual nourishment. Invite your family. Invite your friends. Send it even to the person who does not yet believe.
Not because Gospel Warrior is the destination.
Jesus is.
And remember this when your past whispers your old name:
Jesus does not need to pretend your scandal never happened to prove that His grace can write a greater ending.
